topic: People reached the Americas from Asia at least 15,000 years ago; European colonisation from the 16th century brought disease, war and dispossession to Native peoples.
Thirteen British colonies declared independence in 1776, won it in 1783 and wrote a federal Constitution in 1787.
The young republic expanded west across the continent; the dispute over slavery led to the Civil War (1861–65), which ended slavery and preserved the Union.
Industrialised by 1900, the United States emerged from two world wars as a superpower, led the West in the Cold War, and has been the dominant world power since 1991.

Indigenous period: People crossed from Siberia into North America at least 15,000 years ago and spread across both continents.
Societies ranged from hunter-gatherers to farming peoples; the Mississippian 'Mound Builders' built cities such as Cahokia.
Norse Greenlanders reached Newfoundland around 1000, but left no lasting settlement.
European colonization (1075–1754): Spain founded St. Augustine in Florida (1565); England founded Jamestown, Virginia (1607) and the Pilgrims Plymouth (1620).
The Dutch held New Netherland until England took it in 1664 (renamed New York); France claimed Canada and Louisiana.
The colonies split into New England, the Middle Colonies and the plantation South, where enslaved Africans replaced indentured servants as the main labour force.
Settlement brought repeated wars with Native nations and catastrophic losses to disease.
Revolutionary period (1754–1793): Britain's victory over France in the French and Indian War (1754–63) left debts, and its new taxes provoked colonial protest: 'no taxation without representation'.
After the Boston Tea Party (1773) and fighting at Lexington and Concord (1775), the Second Continental Congress declared independence on 4 July 1776.
With French help the colonies won; Britain recognised independence in the Treaty of Paris (1783).
The Constitutional Convention (1787) created a federal government with separated powers; the Bill of Rights followed in 1791.
Early republic (1793–1830): Washington was the first president (1789–97); Hamilton's financial system, including the First Bank of the United States, divided the first political parties.
Jefferson's Louisiana Purchase (1803) doubled the country's size.
The War of 1812 against Britain ended in a draw but strengthened national feeling; the importation of enslaved people was banned in 1808, while slavery itself spread west.
Expansion and reform (1830–1848): Andrew Jackson's era widened voting for white men and created the Democrats-versus-Whigs 'Second Party System'.
Indian removal forced the Cherokee and other nations west along the 'Trail of Tears'.
'Manifest destiny' drove expansion: Texas was annexed and the Mexican–American War (1846–48) won California and the Southwest.
Civil War and Reconstruction (1848–1877): Whether new territories would allow slavery split the country; Lincoln's election in 1860 led eleven Southern states to secede as the Confederacy.
The Civil War (1861–65) killed about 620,000–750,000 soldiers; Gettysburg (1863) was the turning point, and Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation made it a war against slavery.
Lincoln was assassinated in 1865; the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments abolished slavery and promised citizenship and votes to freed people.
Reconstruction ended in 1877, and white Southern rule returned with segregation and Ku Klux Klan terror.
Gilded Age and the Progressive Era (1877: Railroads, steel and oil made the US the world's largest industrial economy; millions of immigrants arrived, and wealth became highly concentrated.
Progressive reformers, including Theodore Roosevelt, attacked monopolies, corruption and unsafe working conditions.
Victory in the Spanish–American War (1898) brought overseas colonies such as the Philippines and Puerto Rico; the Panama Canal opened in 1914.
Modern America and World Wars (1914–1945: The US entered the First World War in 1917; Wilson's peace plans at Paris were rejected by the Senate.
The 1920s brought Prohibition, women's suffrage and a boom that ended in the Wall Street crash of 1929.
Franklin D. Roosevelt answered the Great Depression with the New Deal.
After Pearl Harbor (1941) the US fought Germany and Japan, built the atomic bomb in the Manhattan Project, and ended the war as the strongest power on earth.
Cold War (1945–1991): The US led the Western bloc against the Soviet Union: the Marshall Plan, NATO, and wars in Korea and Vietnam.
The Cuban Missile Crisis (1962) was the closest the superpowers came to nuclear war; the Space Race ended with the Moon landing in 1969.
At home, the civil rights movement ended legal segregation; the 1960s also brought the Great Society programmes, the counterculture and second-wave feminism.
The Cold War ended with the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991.
Contemporary United States (1991–present: As the sole superpower the US led the Gulf War (1991); the internet economy boomed in the 1990s.
The September 11 attacks (2001) led to wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, the 'War on Terror'.
The 2008 financial crisis, deepening political polarisation and the COVID-19 pandemic marked the following decades.
